nodes.title: Article: Plan mode is dead
nodes.summary: Ayman Nadeem's post-mortem of Nuanced, a plan-first coding app, and why she thinks plan modes are the wrong abstraction.

nodes.title: HN thread: Plan mode is dead
nodes.summary: 291-comment Hacker News discussion (item 49840054, 315 points) where practitioners describe the planning workflows and tools they actually use.

nodes.title: Generated prose is hard to review
nodes.summary: Long AI-written plans and comments bury the decisions that matter; reviewers glaze over, so constrain length and shape of anything a human must read.

nodes.title: Scale ceremony to blast radius
nodes.summary: Skip planning for small reversible changes; require an explicit plan and a human stop for auth, payments, shared schemas, data migrations and prod.

nodes.title: The plan as a context boundary
nodes.summary: A finished plan is a natural point to clear context and start a fresh session; people disagree on whether large context windows made that obsolete.

nodes.title: Never trust a single session
nodes.summary: A second session with no shared context, ideally from another model family, catches errors the author session can't see.

nodes.title: Fix the vocabulary first
nodes.summary: Agree on names for the things in your system before building, so you and the agent mean the same thing and the agent doesn't invent its own terms.

nodes.title: Understand → act → inspect → adjust
nodes.summary: The article's replacement for plan→approve→execute; planning happens inside a tight loop rather than as a gate in front of it.

nodes.title: Modes make you answer a meta-question
nodes.summary: A separate plan mode forces the user to decide up front whether a task deserves planning; letting the phrasing or a project rule decide removes that load.

nodes.title: Plan with a strong model, build with a cheaper one
nodes.summary: Spend the expensive model on planning and review and a cheaper model on execution; the plan file is the handoff.

nodes.title: Plan mode is only a prompt
nodes.summary: Per the Claude Code team, plan mode is a reminder appended to each message, not a sandbox or tool restriction; treat it as convention, not safety.

nodes.title: Planning is not the plan
nodes.summary: The thinking before building is valuable; a large generated plan document usually isn't. Keep the activity, shrink the artifact.

nodes.title: The two jobs of plan mode
nodes.summary: Plan mode did two jobs, making instructions precise for the agent and building human understanding; the first is fading, the second is growing.

nodes.title: Smarter models still can't read minds
nodes.summary: Better models infer more, but intent you never stated (taste, org context, implicit constraints) still has to be elicited; the cheapest place is before code exists.

nodes.title: Keeping the human's mental model current
nodes.summary: The unsolved problem the article ends on; when agents write most of the code, how does the human still understand the system, and how does that scale to many agents?

nodes.title: Adversarial review by a second session
nodes.summary: Have a fresh session (ideally another model family) attack the plan, explanation or diff before you accept it.

nodes.title: Agent-picked tests for slow CI
nodes.summary: When the full test suite takes hours, index which tests touch which code and have an agent pick the relevant tests for each change, with full runs and automatic bisecting on a schedule.

nodes.title: Plan in conversation, no mode
nodes.summary: Say "discuss first, no code yet" (or set a standing phrasing rule) and plan in the normal session; act only on an explicit go.

nodes.title: Agent-written decision log
nodes.summary: Have the agent write a short design note before each non-trivial change and record deviations afterward; you rarely read it, but it's there for forensics.

nodes.title: Decommenting pass before PR
nodes.summary: Strip agent stream-of-consciousness comments before each PR, keeping only comments that explain why; a clean codebase makes future generations cleaner.

nodes.title: Scripts that draw the system from code
nodes.summary: Have the agent write scripts that generate diagrams and tables directly from code or config, so your view of the system can't drift or be hallucinated.

nodes.title: Explainer artifacts attached to PRs
nodes.summary: For complex or core changes, ask for diagrams or an interactive demo explaining the change and the alternatives considered, and attach it to the PR for reviewers and future agents.

nodes.title: Lightweight feasibility check
nodes.summary: Instead of a full plan, ask for a short feasibility verdict and two or three solution options, just enough to confirm the agent's approach matches yours.

nodes.title: You write the spec, the agent asks
nodes.summary: Write the spec by hand and use the agent only to surface questions about it; keeps the spec short, yours, and in your own words.

nodes.title: Make the agent interview you
nodes.summary: Before any plan, have the agent ask you its top questions one at a time until the ambiguities are yours to decide rather than its to guess.

nodes.title: Read-only credentials instead of trust
nodes.summary: Give agents read-only DB users, replicas or copies and no prod secrets, so safety doesn't depend on plan mode or on the model behaving.

nodes.title: Living spec directory and TODO.md
nodes.summary: Keep specs as a directory of files (and a TODO.md of known bugs and future work) that the agent must update whenever something material changes.

nodes.title: Parent theorizes, children execute
nodes.summary: A long-lived parent session holds the plan and the theory; it dispatches narrowly-scoped subagents with only the context they need, and stays available to be quizzed.

nodes.title: Short sessions passing handoff docs
nodes.summary: Break work into phases run by short-lived sessions, each starting from an explicit handoff doc and ending by writing the next one.

nodes.title: Plan mode as a late checkpoint
nodes.summary: Explore and decide in normal conversation first; switch to plan mode only at the end to consolidate one reviewable plan, catch remaining gaps, and clear context before building.

nodes.title: Plan file, then a fresh session
nodes.summary: Iterate on plan.md with the agent, then start a new session that reads only the plan and implements it; the file is audit trail, handoff and context reset in one.

nodes.title: Switch to planning when it spirals
nodes.summary: When the agent starts looping on the same fix, stop execution and make it step back and plan with more thought before touching code again.

nodes.title: Prototype first, architecture later
nodes.summary: Build a quick prototype, name the domain, lock liked behaviour with tests, and refactor into the architecture once real use cases reveal it.

nodes.title: Refactor to make the change easy
nodes.summary: Before building a feature, have the agent remove the cruft the feature would build on, and fold that cleanup into the feature's work.

nodes.title: Skip the plan, review the PR
nodes.summary: When the codebase has strong linters, hooks and patterns, let the agent make a first pass and spend your attention on the diff instead of on a plan you would skim anyway.

nodes.title: Explore, list unknowns, scaffold, spike
nodes.summary: Before real code, require exploration, an explicit list of assumptions, a stub-only scaffold of intent in the codebase, and spikes that validate the risky assumptions.

nodes.title: Challenge the first plan with more research
nodes.summary: After the first plan, send the agent back to research the codebase's own constraints and ask it to improve the plan; first plans are often the first idea that works, not the smallest change.

nodes.title: Re-plan until the spec stops changing
nodes.summary: Run the planning pass over your spec repeatedly, fixing the spec each time, and only implement once a pass finds nothing new.

nodes.title: Throwaway spikes while planning
nodes.summary: While the plan is still a draft, send subagents to implement it in a scratch directory and report back what they learned; the plan stays yours, the spike stays disposable.

nodes.title: Strategy doc, then sprint doc, then build
nodes.summary: For big features, iterate a high-level strategy doc, then a technical sprint doc, then implementation and e2e scenarios, with a human resolving "founder questions" and another model reviewing each stage.

nodes.title: End-to-end tests that carry the plan
nodes.summary: Encode the plan as an end-to-end test harness whose failure messages quote the relevant part of the plan, so long unattended runs stay on track.

nodes.title: HTML explainers and artifacts
nodes.summary: Generated HTML pages, diagrams or interactive demos used to explain a change or hold a plan; shareable and linkable from PRs.

nodes.title: Claude Code question tool
nodes.summary: Built-in tool that lets Claude ask you structured multiple-choice questions in any mode, not only plan mode.

nodes.title: beads
nodes.summary: CLI issue tracker for agents ("Jira for agents"), suggested for managing phased handoffs between short sessions.

nodes.title: Claude Code hooks
nodes.summary: Shell commands the harness runs on events such as before a tool call; can deny edits while a read-only flag is set, which gives plan mode the teeth it lacks.

nodes.title: Claude Code plan mode
nodes.summary: Built-in mode (shift+tab or /plan) that adds a "don't code yet" reminder to each message; plus the hidden setting that restores clear-context-on-accept.

nodes.title: clops-mcp
nodes.summary: SkyPuncher's MCP server acting as a pseudo-harness of stacked multi-step "micro-skills" for repeatable agent workflows (published without the actual ops).

nodes.title: grill-me and grill-with-docs skills
nodes.summary: Matt Pocock's skills that make the agent interview you exhaustively about a feature before building; widely cited as a plan-mode replacement.

nodes.title: imbue-ai/blueprint
nodes.summary: Skill package offered as a plan-mode replacement; mentioned once without detail.

nodes.title: Other tools mentioned (unvetted)
nodes.summary: Products and repos linked in the thread, mostly by their own authors; listed for completeness, not recommended.

nodes.title: opusplan model setting
nodes.summary: Claude Code model alias that uses a stronger model while planning and a cheaper one for execution.

nodes.title: Plannotator
nodes.summary: Web UI for reviewing and annotating agent plans inline, then sending the annotations back; the most-recommended third-party tool in the thread.

nodes.title: Annotation and diff-review UIs
nodes.summary: Tools for commenting on plans and diffs in place — VS Code extension plan annotation, Codex annotations, tuicr and hunk — instead of copy-pasting into chat.

nodes.title: Sandboxes and read-only credentials
nodes.summary: Containers, VMs, DB replicas and read-only users that bound what an agent can break, independent of prompts or modes.

nodes.title: Subagents
nodes.summary: Child agents with their own fresh context, used for isolated review, parallel spikes and per-slice implementation.

nodes.title: obra/superpowers
nodes.summary: Popular skill pack for plan-then-execute workflows; the thread's reviews were mostly negative on bloat and cost.

nodes.title: Anchoring on the first choice
nodes.summary: The agent treats its first decision as fixed, refusing "breaking" changes to uncommitted code or wrapping the old path in defensive code and comments instead of replacing it.

nodes.title: Cargo-cult mega-prompts
nodes.summary: Pages of role-play and procedure ("You are a senior expert reviewer…") that newer models don't need and that crowd out the actual task.

nodes.title: Comments as the agent's scratchpad
nodes.summary: Agents narrate history, conversation and the obvious in code comments; it buries the why and teaches future generations the same habit.

nodes.title: Review loops with no stop rule
nodes.summary: Adversarial review sessions can always find something; without a severity bar or a pass limit they never converge.

nodes.title: Waterfall front-loading
nodes.summary: Forcing all thinking into an up-front spec phase so that going back after implementation starts feels like failure.

nodes.title: Orchestration theater
nodes.summary: Elaborate multi-agent pipelines with boards, gates and personas that look productive while burning tokens and producing little.

nodes.title: Implementation details in the plan
nodes.summary: A planner that hasn't done the deep dive writes code-level detail that the better-informed implementing agent then has to follow or fight.

nodes.title: Trusting the agent's account of its code
nodes.summary: Agent explanations feel complete but omit what the model deemed irrelevant and can be confidently wrong; a feeling of understanding isn't understanding.

nodes.title: Unbounded "looks good, go"
nodes.summary: Approving a plan and letting the agent run overnight without verification gates, budgets or permission limits.
